strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly demonstrated limitation of existing LSNM-based causal discovery methods: misspecification under skewed noise, illustrated convincingly in Fig. 1 and Fig. 3.

Technically sound extension of LSNM to skew-normal noise, with careful derivation of the penalized likelihood and an ECM algorithm adapted from prior statistical literature (Ferreira, Borelli Zeller, and de Oliveira Garcia 2023), including correct handling of the latent-variable representation of the skew-normal distribution.

Sensible practical optimization pipeline combining Bayesian optimization for penalty hyperparameters, CMA-ES for heuristic global search, and ECM refinement, with an ablation (Appendix B) showing the ECM step meaningfully improves accuracy over the heuristic alone, especially for LSNMs (up to 34 points in accuracy).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation, introducing new skew-noise benchmark datasets (ANs/LSs with varying skewness including levels beyond what skew-normal itself can represent) plus 13 established benchmarks, and comparing against a comprehensive set of relevant baselines (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD, CAM, RESIT, IGCI variants).

The identifiability discussion (Sec. 4) appropriately grounds the approach in existing LSNM identifiability theory rather than asserting an unsupported novel identifiability result, and the marginal-likelihood neglect argument for the likelihood-scoring variant is justified with a proposition.
The paper is transparent about implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute in Appendix B, aiding reproducibility, and states code/data availability.
weaknesses: The core contribution is somewhat incremental relative to prior work: it substitutes a normal noise assumption with a skew-normal one within an already-established LSNM framework and largely repurposes an existing ECM algorithm from Ferreira et al. (2023) with modest modifications (spline-based scale, no linear term). The novelty is concentrated in careful engineering/adaptation rather than fundamentally new modeling or theoretical insight.

The skew-normal distribution itself has a bounded maximum skewness (~0.9953), which the paper acknowledges is insufficient to represent the most extreme skew-noise dataset (GNO with γ1≈1.750); yet SKEWD-LL still achieves perfect accuracy there, which is not fully explained mechanistically—it would strengthen the paper to discuss why misspecification in this regime does not hurt cause-effect discrimination, versus relying only on the log-likelihood asymmetry argument implicit in prior work (Schultheiss & Buhlmann).

On the established benchmarks (Table 1), SKEWD does not achieve state-of-the-art performance overall—ROCHE (t-distributed noise) outperforms both SKEWD variants in accuracy and AUDRC by a nontrieal margin, and the paper's claim of being "on par with SOTA" understates this gap, especially given ROCHE's assumption of heavy-tailed rather than skewed noise, which seems more broadly useful on real data.

The experimental section lacks statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests, confidence intervals across datasets) to substantiate whether the accuracy differences between SKEWD and top baselines like ROCHE or LOCI are statistically meaningful, particularly given the large standard deviations reported in Tables 1 and 8.

The synthetic skew-noise datasets are generated using the same functional forms (sigmoidal f, g) and noise families (skew-normal, GNO) that closely mirror the assumed model class of SKEWD, which risks favoring the proposed method; the real-world evaluation is limited to existing established benchmarks without additional domain-specific validation of the skewness assumption in genuinely real (non-synthetic) skewed data beyond citing Genton (2004) examples in the introduction.

The paper does not report runtime/computational cost of SKEWD relative to baselines (e.g., neural-network-based LOCI), despite the multi-stage optimization (Bayesian optimization + CMA-ES + ECM) being potentially expensive; this omission limits practical assessment of scalability.

Limitations discussion is brief and does not address potential failure modes such as noise distributions with skewness or tail behavior outside the skew-normal family's range (beyond the sentence on future heavy-tailed extensions), nor sensitivity to the B-spline knot/dimension choices (q=14, p=7) which are fixed a priori rather than tuned or justified empirically.

strengths: Clear motivation grounded in a real, well-documented limitation of existing LSNM causal discovery methods: Gaussian/symmetric noise assumptions degrade under skewed noise, which the paper convincingly illustrates with Fig. 1/3.

Principled extension of the LSNM framework to skew-normal noise, remaining within the identifiable model class (leveraging existing identifiability results from Immer et al. and Strobl & Lasko) rather than introducing an unjustified heuristic.

Technically careful derivation of a penalized-likelihood estimator and an ECM algorithm adapted from existing statistical literature (Ferreira et al. 2023) to the LSNM spline setting, including an ablation (Appendix B) showing the ECM refinement meaningfully improves over the CMA-ES heuristic alone, which supports the necessity of this design choice.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning both newly constructed skew-noise datasets (with controlled skewness levels via skew-normal and generalized-normal noise) and 13 established benchmarks including the real-world Tübingen pairs, with two complementary inference strategies (likelihood scoring and independence testing).

Honest discussion of limitations (restriction to bivariate case, bounded skewness of skew-normal, Gaussian-marginal assumption for likelihood scoring) and inclusion of a theoretical note on when identifiability holds.
weaknesses: The skewed-noise benchmark used for the headline results is partly generated directly from the skew-normal distribution that SKEWD models, which risks a self-serving evaluation: half of the novel dataset classes (λ=-2, λ=20) exactly match the assumed noise family, inflating apparent superiority over baselines that assume a different (mismatched) family; a cleaner test would rely solely on the GNO-distributed (misspecified for all methods) cases to assess genuine robustness.

On the established, independently curated benchmarks (Tab. 1), SKEWD is not the top performer — ROCHE outperforms both SKEWD variants in accuracy and AUDRC, and LOCI remains highly competitive — undermining the claim of general across-the-board superiority and suggesting the gains are concentrated in the authors' own synthetic setting.

The three-stage estimation pipeline (Bayesian optimization over α, κ with k-fold CV + CMA-ES heuristic search with multiple restarts + ECM refinement) is computationally heavy and stochastic; no runtime/scalability comparison to baselines is provided, and one Tübingen pair required reduced ECM iterations due to dataset size, raising practical scalability concerns not addressed in the main text.

The skew-normal distribution has a hard-bounded skewness (|γ1| < ~0.995), so the method cannot represent highly skewed noise (e.g., γ1 ≈ 1.750 in the GNO datasets) even though it is evaluated there; the reported strong performance in this clearly misspecified regime is not fully explained mechanistically, raising questions about whether the comparative gains generalize to even more extreme real-world skewness.

The likelihood-scoring variant depends on an asymptotic approximation (Proposition 1) assuming marginals are standardized to look approximately standard normal; this assumption is untested on real data (e.g., Tübingen) where marginals can be arbitrarily shaped, which could undermine the soundness of likelihood-based inference in practice despite the strong theoretical framing.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting at the level of individual skew-noise dataset comparisons (only point accuracies in Tabs. 4–5), making it hard to assess whether reported differences vs. ROCHE/LOCI are meaningful or within noise, especially given n=100 pairs per condition.

The core technical contribution is largely an application/adaptation of pre-existing skew-normal ECM machinery (Ferreira et al. 2023) and standard CMA-ES/Bayesian optimization to the LSNM setting, which somewhat limits methodological novelty relative to the adjacent literature already using heavy-tailed/Student-t noise (ROCHE) or skewness-based criteria (Lin et al. 2024).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly identified gap: existing LSNM causal discovery methods assume symmetric (typically Gaussian) noise, and the paper convincingly demonstrates via Fig. 1 and subsequent experiments that this leads to misspecification and wrong causal direction inference under skewed noise.

The extension to skew-normal LSNMs is a natural and principled generalization that includes the normal distribution as a special case, preserving compatibility with prior identifiability theory (Immer et al. 2023; Strobl and Lasko 2023) while covering a strictly larger model class.

Careful parameter estimation procedure: the paper identifies real optimization challenges specific to skew-normal likelihoods (non-finite maxima, stationary points at lambda=0) and addresses them with a sensible combination of Bayesian-optimized penalization, CMA-ES heuristic search, and an ECM refinement step derived from prior statistical literature (Ferreira, Borelli Zeller, and de Oliveira Garcia 2023), adapted appropriately to the LSNM setting.

Thorough empirical evaluation: novel synthetic datasets spanning several skewness levels (via both skew-normal and generalized normal noise), combined with 13 established benchmarks (synthetic and real-world Tubingen), and comparisons against a comprehensive set of strong baselines (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD, CAM, RESIT, IGCI).

Useful ablation study (Appendix B) isolating the contribution of the ECM refinement step versus the CMA-ES heuristic alone, which convincingly shows the refinement is necessary, especially for independence-based inference in LSNM settings.
Good attention to reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter settings, computational environment, and stated code availability.

Honest treatment of limitations, explicitly noting restriction to bivariate models, bounded skewness range of the skew-normal distribution, and the normality assumption on marginals used to simplify likelihood scoring.
weaknesses: The skew-normal distribution has a bounded skewness (|γ1| < ~0.995), so SKEWD cannot represent highly skewed noise; the paper's own GNO(0,1,-0.5) dataset (γ1≈1.75) exceeds this range, yet SKEWD still performs best there, raising questions about why/how robustness is achieved despite model misspecification relative to the true generating noise, which is not analyzed in depth.

On the established benchmark suite, SKEWD is not clearly state-of-the-art: ROCHE achieves higher mean accuracy and AUDRC (Table 1), and the gap between SKEWD-IT and ROCHE (2.67%) is not tested for statistical significance, making the 'on par with SOTA' claim only partially substantiated.

The simplification used for likelihood scoring (neglecting marginal log-likelihoods) relies on an asymptotic normality argument via standardization (Proposition 1) that is somewhat informal and may not hold well in finite samples, particularly when the actual marginal X distribution departs from normality (e.g., under hierarchical sigma sampling or skewed causes), which is not empirically validated.

The synthetic data generating mechanisms are restricted to sigmoidal f/g functions following prior work (Tagasovska et al. 2020), limiting the diversity of functional forms tested and potentially favoring methods tuned to this function class.

No runtime/computational cost comparison is provided despite the method combining Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and ECM, which is likely considerably more expensive than simpler baselines (e.g., LOCI, GRCI); this omission limits practical assessment of the method's scalability.
The paper is restricted to the bivariate case, as acknowledged, which limits its immediate applicability to larger causal graphs without further extension (left as future work).

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and under-studied gap: the symmetric-noise assumption in LSNM causal discovery methods, with a concrete illustrative failure case (Figure 1) showing how misspecification propagates to residual dependence and wrong direction inference.

Solid theoretical grounding: builds on established LSNM identifiability results (Immer et al. 2023; Strobl & Lasko 2023) and proves a non-trivial proposition (5.1) justifying that only partial DAG likelihoods need to be compared in the multivariate MEC-scoring extension, which is both correct and practically useful for reducing computation.

Careful treatment of a genuinely difficult estimation problem: skew-normal MLE is known to be numerically delicate (stationary points, unbounded likelihood), and the paper's combination of penalized GAM likelihood, Bayesian-optimized penalty selection, CMA-ES heuristic initialization, and an adapted ECM refinement step is a thoughtful, well-justified pipeline, with an ablation (Appendix B.3) explicitly showing the value of the ECM refinement step.

Extensive empirical evaluation: novel skew-noise benchmarks with controlled/varying skewness (both skew-normal and generalized-normal noise, the latter exceeding the model's own theoretical skewness range) plus 13 established benchmarks (Tübingen, SIM variants, cause-effect challenge datasets), giving a fairly comprehensive picture of when the method helps and when it does not.

Reasonable and honest limitations discussion, including explicit acknowledgment that SKEWD-LL's Gaussian-marginal assumption can be violated, scalability concerns for the multivariate extension (PCC growth), and identifiability caveats; supplemental KDE-marginal ablation transparently reports where it helps and hurts rather than cherry-picking.

Multivariate extension is non-trivial and evaluated with an oracle-MEC ablation (SKEWD-MV-O) that cleanly separates PC-algorithm/MEC-estimation error from the likelihood-scoring contribution, strengthening the causal claims about where errors originate.
weaknesses: On the established (non-skewed-noise) benchmarks, SKEWD does not clearly dominate: ROCHE outperforms both SKEWD variants in mean accuracy and AUDRC in Table 1, and SKEWD-LL performs poorly on the real-world Tübingen benchmark (45.97% accuracy, near chance level), which is a fairly important benchmark for practical relevance and undercuts the 'on par with SOTA' claim in some settings.

The likelihood-scoring variant relies on a Gaussian-marginal assumption for computational convenience (Prop A.1); when this is violated (as on Tübingen or SIM datasets), performance drops substantially, and while a KDE-based fix is explored, it is relegated to an appendix ablation and not integrated as a principal contribution or adaptively selected based on marginal diagnostics.

The skew-normal distribution has an inherent bounded skewness range (|γ1| < ~0.995), so the model is still fundamentally limited for highly skewed real-world noise; the paper's own GNO(1.750) experiments exceed this bound, and while results remain reasonable there, this is a structural limitation of the chosen distributional family that is somewhat downplayed relative to its practical importance.

The multivariate extension (SKEWD-MV) is only evaluated on small synthetic graphs (d=6, d=10) with correctly-specified skew-normal LSNM data generation; there is no real-world multivariate evaluation, and the explicitly acknowledged exponential scaling in undirected-edge count (PCC growth) suggests limited applicability beyond small/moderately dense graphs.

Computational cost of SKEWD relative to baselines (wall-clock runtime) is not reported quantitatively anywhere in the main text or appendix, despite the method involving nested CMA-ES + Bayesian optimization + ECM, which is likely to be considerably more expensive than neural-network-based competitors like LOCI; this omission makes it hard to assess practical trade-offs.

CAREFL is excluded from the main comparison based on default hyperparameters performing poorly on established benchmarks, which risks an unfair comparison against a reasonably strong nonparametric competitor; a more tuned comparison would strengthen the paper's positioning against fully flexible alternatives.

The independence-testing variant (SKEWD-IT), which the paper itself argues is generally more robust than likelihood scoring (citing Immer et al. and Sun & Schulte), still degrades noticeably on the harder skewed LSNM datasets (e.g., 82% on LSs(0.985), 92% on LSs(1.750)), indicating the method does not fully solve the skewness problem for this variant, somewhat tempering the 'consistently performs well' framing in Figure 2's caption.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and underexplored gap in the LSNM causal discovery literature: nearly all prior bivariate/multivariate LSNM methods assume symmetric noise, and the paper provides a clear motivating illustration (Figure 1) of how this misspecification propagates into residual dependence and wrong causal-direction inference.

The technical development is substantial: the skew-normal LSNM is embedded in a GAM framework with B-spline penalization, and a carefully derived ECM algorithm (building on Ferreira et al. 2023) is provided with explicit E-step and CM-step update equations, including a sensible heuristic (CMA-ES + Bayesian-optimized penalty selection) to address the well-known difficulty of skew-normal likelihood optimization.

Experimental coverage is extensive: 13 established bivariate benchmarks plus newly constructed skew-noise datasets (with both skew-normal and generalized-normal noise, the latter testing robustness to model misspecification), as well as a multivariate proof-of-concept against HOST, GraN-DAG++, and CAM.

Useful ablations are included (ECM refinement vs. heuristic-only CMA-ES solution; parametric vs. KDE marginal estimation; oracle vs. estimated MEC in the multivariate setting), which help clarify where the gains actually come from and where the method's assumptions bind.

A formal proposition (5.1) that reduces multivariate DAG scoring to only the unoriented sub-structure is a nice, correctly proven simplification that meaningfully reduces computation within the MEC-based scoring scheme.
Reasonable effort toward reproducibility and honest limitations discussion (scalability caveats, discussion of KDE marginal trade-offs, note on misspecification risks in Section 5.4).
weaknesses: The central 'robust / on-par-with-SOTA' claim is not well supported by the paper's own numbers: on the 13 established benchmarks (Table 1), ROCHE outperforms both SKEWD-LL and SKEWD-IT in both accuracy and AUDRC, and SKEWD-LL in particular trails LOCI-LL-level and QCCD-level performance in several places; SKEWD is at best 'competitive', not dominant, which undercuts the framing of the contribution as a reliable general-purpose improvement.

The newly proposed skew-noise benchmark is partly self-serving: two of the five noise settings are generated directly from the skew-normal distribution that SKEWD assumes, so SKEWD-LL trivially achieves ~100% accuracy in a well-specified regime that exactly matches its own parametric model. This inflates the apparent advantage and makes the 'skewness-robust' narrative less convincing than it appears; the GNO-based settings are a better test of misspecification robustness but are not emphasized as such.

Scalability is a significant practical limitation that is somewhat downplayed: the multivariate method requires fitting a skew-normal regression (full CMA-ES + ECM pipeline) for every parent-child configuration in the estimated MEC, restricting applicability to small graphs (d ≤ 10, PCCs in the order of 100); no wall-clock runtime comparisons against baselines are reported anywhere in the main text.

The large discrepancy between SKEWD-MV and the oracle-MEC variant SKEWD-MV-O (e.g., SHD 2.27 vs 0.14 at d=6) indicates that most of the realistic multivariate error stems from PC-based MEC estimation rather than the proposed skew-normal scoring itself, suggesting the core multivariate contribution is more modest than the oracle results imply.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the head-to-head comparisons despite substantial standard deviations (e.g., ~20% accuracy std in Table 9), making it hard to assess whether reported differences between SKEWD and ROCHE/LOCI/GRCI are meaningful or within noise.

The skew-normal assumption itself is fairly restrictive (bounded skewness ~0.995, bounded excess kurtosis ~0.87), and the paper's own experiments show degrading performance under heavier-tailed/more skewed GNO noise relative to ROCHE's t-distribution-based approach, somewhat contradicting the 'robust under skewed noise' positioning in the title and abstract.

Presentation relies heavily on the appendix for essential technical and empirical content (full derivations, all per-dataset numbers, KDE ablation, identifiability restatement), which makes it difficult to assess robustness of claims from the main text alone and suggests the contribution may be overstuffed for a single paper.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: the symmetry assumption on noise in LSNMs is shown empirically and conceptually to degrade performance under realistic skewed noise, and the paper provides a clear illustrative example (Figure 1) of the failure mode.

Solid technical contribution: a full skew-normal LSNM is formalized, combined with GAM-based flexible f/g functions, a penalized likelihood, and a carefully adapted ECM algorithm (building on but non-trivially extending Ferreira et al.) with a two-stage heuristic+ECM optimization strategy to deal with the known difficulties of skew-normal MLE.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: both independence-testing and likelihood-scoring variants are tested against a large number of strong baselines (LOCI, ROCHE, GRCI, QCCD, CAM, RESIT, IGCI, CAREFL) on 13 established benchmarks plus newly constructed skew-noise datasets with controlled, varying skewness (including both skew-normal and generalized-normal noise for robustness checks beyond the assumed family).

Useful ablations in the appendix (ECM vs. heuristic-only estimates, Gaussian vs. KDE marginals) that support specific design choices and are honestly reported even when KDE sometimes outperforms the proposed Gaussian-marginal assumption.

Proposition 5.1 gives a theoretically justified computational shortcut for the multivariate likelihood-scoring extension (scoring only nodes with unoriented edges), which is a nice, practically relevant result with a correct, included proof.

Reasonable care with reproducibility and limitations: detailed appendix on implementation/hyperparameters, explicit identifiability caveats, and an honest discussion of scalability constraints for the multivariate extension.
weaknesses: On the 13 established (non-adversarially-skewed) benchmarks, SKEWD is only competitive rather than dominant—ROCHE actually has the best mean accuracy/AUDRC overall (Table 1), and on the real-world Tübingen benchmark SKEWD's accuracy (66.57% IT, 45.97% LL) is mediocre and below several baselines, somewhat undercutting the claim of being 'the most reliable approach.'

The main skewed-noise benchmarks on which SKEWD dominates are synthetic datasets constructed by the authors themselves using skew-normal/GNO noise, which is very close to the model family SKEWD assumes; this creates a risk that the headline results partly reflect a favorable match between data-generating process and model rather than a fully independent stress test (the GNO robustness check partially, but not fully, mitigates this).

The multivariate extension (SKEWD-MV) is only validated on small graphs (d=6, 10) with favorable MEC structure, relies on the PC algorithm for the equivalence class (introducing an additional, unmodeled source of error when M̂ is wrong), and the independence-testing variant is not extended to the multivariate setting at all, leaving a gap in the method's completeness.

Computational cost appears high (Bayesian optimization + multi-start CMA-ES + ECM refinement per direction/model), and while scalability is discussed qualitatively (PCC counts), no wall-clock runtime comparisons against baselines are reported, making practical efficiency hard to assess.

The skew-normal has bounded maximum skewness (~0.995) and bounded kurtosis, yet real-world or more extreme skewed phenomena (as motivated in the intro, e.g., financial/environmental data) may exceed this; the paper's own GNO(k=-0.5) experiment already pushes beyond the theoretical range, and while results are encouraging, the degree of robustness in truly heavy-tailed/extremely skewed practical settings remains only partially characterized.

No single recommended variant: SKEWD-LL and SKEWD-IT trade off differently across benchmarks (e.g., LL excels on the skew-noise sets while IT is more robust on established benchmarks), which may complicate practical adoption without clearer guidance on variant selection.
